Antennas on this aircraft · tap to fly there

    The Citation and the 210D carry the antennas the narrator points out on them in the AIM Charlotte video; items tagged FAA fig were added from the knowledge-test figures. The video names only the Seneca's VOR, so the rest of the Seneca (tagged typical) is a normal light-twin fit placed with the FAA figures. The Learjet 25D (N600GM, the jet in the AIM Hasbrouck Heights hangar) is not in the video: it carries every antenna type from the video and the FAA figures in one airframe, each placed from the Learjet 25 maintenance manual (tagged manual, with the chapter quoted on the card) or at the usual retrofit spot (typical). It has no combined VOR/glideslope: the Learjet uses fin-side VOR/LOC half-loops plus two dedicated glideslope antennas in the radome. Names, frequencies and jobs were checked against FAA-H-8083-31B (2023) Chapter 11 and AC 43.13-1B CHG 1 Chapter 12 — each card quotes the passage it rests on. Confirm against the maintenance manual and wiring diagram before touching one.

      FAA knowledge-test figures · Airframe appendix

      All 17 antenna drawings in the Airman Knowledge Testing Supplement (FAA-CT-8080-4G): Figure 16 (four antennas) and Figures 22–34, all in the Airframe appendix (Appendix 3 of this edition; Appendix 2, Powerplant, has none). Each is cropped and keyed with the FAA's answer and linked to its antenna on the models. The only other antenna item in the supplement is Figure 15, the drag formula D = 0.000327 × A × V² (lb, sq ft, mph) used for antenna-load questions.

      Keyed answers are from the published question bank (check them against your own Prepware). Figure 23 is drawn as a TCAS directional plate, so it sits on top of the Citation as TCAS — but its key is "altitude encoder used with transponders", with "TCAS receiver" as a wrong-answer choice, so the encoder is also drawn inside the nose. There is no GPS drawing: Figure 22 looks like a GPS puck but is keyed "loop and sense antenna" (ADF) and is fitted on the Seneca belly as the combined ADF antenna.

      Four rules that put every antenna where it is

      ↑
      Talks to the sky → on topGPS and ELT need a clear view upward. COM 1 goes up top too for the best line of sight to towers.
      ↓
      Talks to the ground → on the bellyTransponder (ground radar), DME (ground station), marker beacon (fans rising from the runway), radio altimeter (straight down), ADF loop. COM 2 often rides underneath for coverage when the aircraft banks.
      →
      Looks ahead → in the noseWeather radar needs an unobstructed view forward, so it lives behind a dielectric radome. On jets the glideslope antenna usually shares the radome.
      〰
      Long wavelength → long structureHF (2–30 MHz) uses the whole fin as the radiator through a coupler behind the leading edge; the ADF sense antenna is a wire the length of the fuselage.

      Transponder or DME?

      Both are short L-band blades on the belly and people mix them up. Seen from the side, the DME blade is narrower; the transponder blade is the wider, stubbier one. When in doubt, follow the coax to the rack.
